title: Priority shelves and deferred-response fallthrough for burst protection
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a hybrid load-shedding mechanism that combines small per-tenant 'priority shelves' (reserved short-lived fast slots) with a deferred-response fallthrough path that returns partial responses or lightweight acknowledgements when SLO thresholds are threatened. The feature aims to reduce p99 latency spikes during bursty traffic while preserving overall throughput and minimizing catastrophic failures during multi-region failover.

Background: We've observed recurring p99 regressions during sudden tenant traffic spikes and region failovers. Current options (hard rejection, simple token-bucket admission) either result in high error rates or punitive rejection of high-value requests. Priority shelves provide bounded, pre-authorized fast-path capacity for latency-sensitive requests; deferred-response fallthrough converts lower-priority requests into partial or async flows to keep the runtime responsive.

Design summary:
- Priority shelves: per-tenant small slot pools (configurable count and TTL) allocated by policy. Shelves are consumed for requests marked latency-sensitive (e.g., short deadline header). Unused shelves expire quickly to prevent resource hoarding. Shelves are formalized as soft reservations layered on top of existing token buckets so they don't bypass fairness.
- Deferred-response fallthrough: when a request cannot be admitted to execution within configured latency budget, the router can either (A) return a structured partial response (first N tokens + continuation token) or (B) convert to an async job that completes later with a webhook or polling handle. Policies are configurable per-route/tenant and tied to SLO class (gold/silver/bronze).
- Multi-region behavior: during regional failover, shelves are rebalanced via leader-coordinated reallocation (fast path) while the deferred path switches to cross-region queueing with capacity-aware rate limits.
- Metrics and SLOs: new metrics (shelf_hit_rate, shelf_evictions, deferred_rate, partial_completion_success) feed into an SLO: target p99 latency for 'gold' class <= 300ms during normal ops and <= 750ms during failover, with deferred_rate capped at 8% for gold tenants.

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs. benefit: priority shelves add bookkeeping overhead—we limit shelf count per tenant and TTL to bound state and GC costs.
- Fairness: to avoid starving small tenants we make shelves optional and tied to billing/tenant tier; default policy provides minimal free shelves to all tenants.
- Data consistency in multi-region reallocation: chose leader-coordinated ephemeral leases over fully synchronous global allocation to reduce tail-latency impact. This introduces short windows where shelf counts may be slightly inconsistent across regions but preserves availability.

Acceptance criteria:
- Shelf mechanism implemented in runtime and router with unit/integration tests for allocation/eviction.
- Deferred-response paths available with structured first-chunk + continuation token and async webhook mode.
- End-to-end benchmark showing p99 improvement of at least 25% for gold workloads under synthetic bursts, and deferred_rate < 8% for gold in tests.
- Dashboards with new metrics and alerting rules.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary runtime + router feature flag in a small internal namespace, run synthetic burst tests (2 days).
2) Gradual enable for selected gold tenants with observability runbook.
3) Wider rollout to all tenants as default, with per-tenant opt-out.

Operational notes: Add a 'shelf_eviction' audit log entry to aid post-incident review. Include a small CLI tool for ops to view shelf allocations by tenant and revoke in emergencies.
